subsections.title: INTRODUCTION TO AI AND INTELLIGENT AGENTS

topics.title: Foundations & Perspectives of AI
topics.content:
Artificial Intelligence Concepts:
- Term coined by John McCarthy (1956, Dartmouth Conference).
- Core Goal: Making machines perform tasks requiring human intelligence.
- Four Perspectives: Thinking Humanly (cognitive modeling), Acting Humanly (Turing Test), Thinking Rationally (laws of thought), Acting Rationally (rational agent approach - modern AI focus).
- Rational Action: Focuses on achieving optimal outcomes/doing the right thing.

topics.title: Intelligent Agents & PEAS Framework
topics.content:
Agent Structure & Properties:
- Agent Cycle: Sensors $\rightarrow$ Percepts $\rightarrow$ Agent Function $\rightarrow$ Actions $\rightarrow$ Actuators.
- Core Properties: Autonomy, Reactivity, Pro-activeness, Social Ability.

PEAS Framework:
- Performance Measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
- Example (Self-Driving Car): P (Safety, speed, comfort), E (Roads, traffic, weather), A (Steering, accelerator, brakes), S (Cameras, GPS, sensors).

topics.title: Agent Architectures & Environment Types
topics.content:
Agent Types (Simple to Complex):
- Simple Reflex Agent: Condition-action rules ("if-then"); no memory; requires fully observable environments.
- Model-Based Reflex Agent: Internal state/memory; handles partially observable environments.
- Goal-Based Agent: Considers future consequences and planning to achieve explicit goals.
- Utility-Based Agent: Evaluates state desirability via a utility function; balances conflicting trade-offs.

Environment Dimensions:
- Fully Observable vs. Partially Observable.
- Deterministic vs. Stochastic (stochastic involves randomness).
- Static vs. Dynamic (dynamic changes during deliberation).
- Discrete vs. Continuous.
- Single Agent vs. Multi-Agent (competitive or cooperative).

topics.title: Problem Formulation & Uninformed Search
topics.content:
State Space Search Formulation:
- Components: Initial State, Actions/Operators, Goal Test, Path Cost Function.
- Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP): Variables, Domains, Constraints.

Uninformed (Blind) Search Strategies:
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): Explores level-by-level using a Queue (FIFO); Complete and Optimal for unit step costs; Time/Space Complexity: $O(b^d)$.
- Depth-First Search (DFS): Explores deep branches using a Stack (LIFO); Not Complete/Optimal; Space Complexity: $O(b \times m)$.
- Depth-Limited Search (DLS): DFS with a depth limit $L$ to prevent infinite paths.
- Iterative Deepening Search (IDS): Combines BFS optimality/completeness with DFS space efficiency $O(b \times d)$.
- Bidirectional Search: Searches simultaneously from start and goal; Time/Space Complexity: $O(b^{d/2})$.

topics.title: Informed Search & Local Search Algorithms
topics.content:
Informed (Heuristic) Search:
- Greedy Best-First Search: Uses $f(n) = h(n)$; fast but neither complete nor optimal.
- A* Search: Uses $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$ where $g(n)$ is actual cost and $h(n)$ is estimated cost to goal. Complete and Optimal if $h(n)$ is Admissible (never overestimates true cost) and Consistent.

Local Search & Optimization:
- Hill Climbing: Greedy local search; prone to local maxima, plateaus, and ridges.
- Simulated Annealing: Escapes local maxima by accepting worse moves with probability $e^{\Delta E / T}$; temperature $T$ decreases over time.

topics.title: Game Playing & Adversarial Search
topics.content:
Game Playing Fundamentals:
- Two-player zero-sum games with perfect information.
- Minimax Algorithm: Evaluates game trees by maximizing MAX's outcome and minimizing MIN's outcome; Time Complexity: $O(b^m)$.
- Alpha-Beta Pruning: Optimizes Minimax without altering results by tracking $\alpha$ (MAX's best) and $\beta$ (MIN's best); Best-case time complexity: $O(b^{m/2})$.

topics.title: Structured Representation & Propositional Logic
topics.content:
KR Approaches & Trade-offs:
- Expressive Adequacy, Inferential Adequacy, Inferential Efficiency.
- Semantic Networks: Graphs with nodes (concepts) and edges (IS-A, HAS-A, INSTANCE-OF) supporting property inheritance.
- Frames: Object-like structures introduced by Marvin Minsky using slots, facets, and default values.

Propositional Logic (PL):
- Connectives: Negation ($\neg$), Conjunction ($\wedge$), Disjunction ($\vee$), Implication ($\rightarrow$), Biconditional ($\leftrightarrow$).
- $P \rightarrow Q \equiv \neg P \vee Q$ (False only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false).
- Formulas: Tautology (always true), Contradiction (always false), Satisfiable (true for at least one interpretation).
- Inference Rules: Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Resolution.
- Resolution Refutation: Proof by contradiction using Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) to derive an empty clause ($\square$).

topics.title: First-Order Predicate Logic & Probabilistic Reasoning
topics.content:
First-Order Predicate Logic (FOPL):
- Extends PL with Constants, Variables, Predicates, Functions, and Quantifiers: Universal ($\forall$), Existential ($\exists$).
- Quantifier Negation: $\neg(\forall x P(x)) \equiv \exists x \neg P(x)$ and $\neg(\exists x P(x)) \equiv \forall x \neg P(x)$.
- Unification: Finding substitutions (Unifiers/MGU) to make predicate expressions identical.

Probabilistic Reasoning:
- Bayes' Rule: $P(A|B) = \frac{P(B|A) \times P(A)}{P(B)}$.
- Bayesian Networks: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) where nodes represent random variables and conditional probability tables (CPT) manage probabilistic dependencies.

subsections.title: EXPERT SYSTEMS, NLP, VISION AND ROBOTICS

topics.title: Expert Systems & Knowledge Engineering
topics.content:
Expert Systems Architecture:
- Key Modules: Knowledge Base (rules/facts), Inference Engine, Working Memory, User Interface, Explanation Facility. Knowledge acquisition is a primary bottleneck.
- Forward Chaining: Data-driven (facts $\rightarrow$ conclusions); used for diagnosis.
- Backward Chaining: Goal-driven (goal $\rightarrow$ supporting facts); used for hypothesis verification.
- Knowledge Types: Declarative (knowing WHAT / facts) vs. Procedural (knowing HOW / methods).
- Classic Examples: MYCIN (bacterial medical diagnosis), DENDRAL, XCON.

topics.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
topics.content:
NLP Concepts & Pipeline:
- NLU (Natural Language Understanding: text to meaning) vs. NLG (Natural Language Generation: meaning to text).
- NLP Pipeline: Lexical Analysis (tokenization) $\rightarrow$ Syntactic Analysis (parsing parse trees) $\rightarrow$ Semantic Analysis (meaning extraction) $\rightarrow$ Discourse Integration $\rightarrow$ Pragmatic Analysis (context/intent).
- Core Challenges: Lexical, syntactic, and semantic ambiguity; context dependence.

topics.title: Computer Vision & Robotics
topics.content:
Machine Vision & Robotics:
- Machine Vision Pipeline: Image Acquisition $\rightarrow$ Preprocessing $\rightarrow$ Segmentation (edge detection) $\rightarrow$ Feature Extraction $\rightarrow$ Recognition/Classification $\rightarrow$ Scene Interpretation.
- Robotics: Embodied AI operating in a Sense-Think-Act loop using sensors, actuators, control systems, and power supplies.

topics.title: Types of Learning & Decision Trees
topics.content:
Machine Learning Paradigms:
- Supervised Learning: Learns from labeled data; includes Classification (discrete targets) and Regression (continuous targets).
- Unsupervised Learning: Finds patterns in unlabeled data; includes Clustering (K-Means) and Dimensionality Reduction (PCA).
- Reinforcement Learning: Trial-and-error learning via Agent, State, Action, Policy, and Rewards/Penalties.

Decision Trees (ID3 / C4.5):
- Attribute selection uses Information Gain: $IG(S, A) = \text{Entropy}(S) - \sum \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \text{Entropy}(S_v)$.
- Entropy Formula: $H(S) = -\sum p_i \log_2(p_i)$ ($H=0$ for pure sets, $H=1$ for equal mix).
- Overfitting mitigation: Tree pruning.

topics.title: Naive Bayes, Fuzzy Systems & Genetic Algorithms
topics.content:
Naive Bayes Classifier:
- Based on Bayes' Theorem with the "naive" assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class. Uses Laplace Smoothing for zero-frequency problems.

Fuzzy Logic & Inference (FIS):
- Fuzzy Sets: Membership values in continuous range $[0, 1]$.
- Operators: AND = $\min(A, B)$, OR = $\max(A, B)$, NOT = $1 - A$.
- FIS Pipeline: Fuzzification $\rightarrow$ Rule Base Evaluation $\rightarrow$ Defuzzification (Centroid method; Mamdani or Sugeno inference).

Genetic Algorithms (GA):
- Evolutionary optimization inspired by natural selection.
- Components: Population, Chromosomes, Fitness Function.
- Operators: Selection (Roulette Wheel, Tournament, Rank), Crossover (Single-point, Two-point, Uniform), Mutation (Bit flip, Swap).

topics.title: ANN Foundations & Activation Functions
topics.content:
Artificial Neural Networks (ANN):
- Biological Inspiration: Dendrites (inputs), Soma (summation), Axon (output), Synapses (weights).
- McCulloch-Pitts Neuron (1943): Binary inputs/outputs with fixed threshold.
- Mathematical Neuron Model: $y = f(\sum w_i x_i + b) = f(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b)$.

Activation Functions:
- Step Function: Binary threshold.
- Sigmoid: $\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$, range $(0, 1)$.
- Tanh: $\tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}$, range $(-1, 1)$.
- ReLU: $f(x) = \max(0, x)$, range $[0, \infty)$.
- Leaky ReLU: $f(x) = \max(\alpha x, x)$.
- Softmax: Multi-class output probability distribution summing to 1.

topics.title: Perceptrons & Training Optimization
topics.content:
Perceptron & Optimization:
- Single-layer Perceptron: Classifies linearly separable problems; fails on non-linearly separable problems like XOR.
- Learning Rate ($\eta$): Controls weight update step size.
- Gradient Descent: Minimizes loss function via $w_{new} = w_{old} - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$. Variants: Batch GD, Stochastic GD (SGD), Mini-Batch GD.
- Delta Rule / Widrow-Hoff Rule: Gradient descent learning for continuous activation functions.
- Backpropagation: Trains Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) by propagating error signals backward.
- Hebbian Learning: "Neurons that fire together, wire together" ($\Delta w = \eta \cdot x \cdot y$).
- Hopfield Network: Recurrent associative memory network.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a foundation of Artificial Intelligence?
questions.explanation: Astrology is a pseudoscience and is not a foundational field of Artificial Intelligence[cite: 1].

questions.question: The term 'Artificial Intelligence' was first coined by:
questions.explanation: John McCarthy first coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference[cite: 1].

questions.question: Which agent type uses a model of the world to handle partial observability?
questions.explanation: A Model-Based Reflex Agent maintains internal state memory to keep track of unobserved world aspects[cite: 1].

questions.question: In PEAS description, 'E' stands for:
questions.explanation: PEAS stands for Performance Measure, Environment, Actuators, and Sensors[cite: 1].

questions.question: An agent that selects actions based on current percept only, using condition-action rules is:
questions.explanation: Simple Reflex Agents operate purely on the current percept using condition-action ('if-then') rules[cite: 1].

questions.question: Which type of agent considers 'how happy it will be' if a certain action is taken?
questions.explanation: Utility-Based Agents use a utility function to measure degree of success or state desirability[cite: 1].

questions.question: An environment where the next state is completely determined by the current state and action is called:
questions.explanation: In a deterministic environment, the subsequent state is fully dictated by the current state and executed action[cite: 1].

questions.question: Chess is an example of which type of environment?
questions.explanation: Chess features fixed non-random rules (deterministic) and involves opposing players (multi-agent)[cite: 1].

questions.question: A taxi driving environment is best described as:
questions.explanation: Driving involves real-time changes during deliberation (dynamic) and unpredictable traffic or weather conditions (stochastic)[cite: 1].

questions.question: Which environment changes while the agent is deliberating?
questions.explanation: A dynamic environment continuously updates its state while an agent decides its next action[cite: 1].

questions.question: In which environment can the agent sense all relevant aspects of the environment?
questions.explanation: A fully observable environment allows agent sensors to access the complete state relevant to decision-making[cite: 1].

questions.question: An intelligent agent must have:
questions.explanation: An agent perceives its environment using sensors and acts upon it using actuators[cite: 1].

questions.question: BFS is implemented using which data structure?
questions.explanation: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores nodes level-by-level using a FIFO Queue[cite: 1].

questions.question: DFS is implemented using which data structure?
questions.explanation: Depth-First Search (DFS) explores deep paths using a LIFO Stack[cite: 1].

questions.question: Which search algorithm is complete but not optimal?
questions.explanation: DFS can be complete in finite spaces, but it is not optimal because it may return a non-shortest solution path[cite: 1].

questions.question: Time complexity of BFS with branching factor b and depth d is:
questions.explanation: The worst-case time complexity of BFS is $O(b^d)$[cite: 1].

questions.question: Which search algorithm combines the benefits of BFS and DFS?
questions.explanation: Iterative Deepening Search (IDS) combines the optimality/completeness of BFS with the memory efficiency $O(b \times d)$ of DFS[cite: 1].

questions.question: A* algorithm uses which evaluation function?
questions.explanation: A* search evaluates nodes using $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, combining actual cost $g(n)$ and estimated goal cost $h(n)$[cite: 1].

questions.question: In A* search, g(n) represents:
options: Actual cost from start to n
questions.explanation: In A* search, $g(n)$ denotes the exact path cost accumulated from the start node to node $n$[cite: 1].

questions.question: Greedy Best-First Search uses evaluation function:
questions.explanation: Greedy Best-First Search ranks nodes solely using heuristic estimates $f(n) = h(n)$[cite: 1].
